theme: Moses and Aaron sent; the plagues recounted
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 105:26-45. This is the exodus story told as praise. Compare it in your mind to Psalm 106, which you read earlier in the unit. The two psalms tell the same history from opposite sides.
settingTheScene: Psalm 105 and Psalm 106 are a pair. Psalm 106 tells the story of Israel’s failures. Psalm 105 tells the story of God’s faithfulness. This psalm begins by calling Israel to thank the LORD and make his deeds known among the peoples, and then it traces the history from Abraham to the conquest. Today you read the section about the exodus, and it is a fitting way to end Unit 5, since it summarizes everything you have just read and gives the reason for it.
observation: “He sent Moses his servant, and Aaron, whom he had chosen” (v. 26).
“They performed his signs among them and miracles in the land of Ham” (v. 27).
The plagues are recounted: darkness, blood, frogs, flies, gnats, hail, locusts, and the death of the firstborn (vv. 28-36).
“Then he brought out Israel with silver and gold, and there was none among his tribes who stumbled” (v. 37).
“Egypt was glad when they departed, for dread of them had fallen upon it” (v. 38).
“He spread a cloud for a covering, and fire to give light by night” (v. 39).
“They asked, and he brought quail, and gave them bread from heaven in abundance” (v. 40).
“He opened the rock, and water gushed out; it flowed through the desert like a river” (v. 41).
“For he remembered his holy promise, and Abraham, his servant” (v. 42).
“So he brought his people out with joy, his chosen ones with singing” (v. 43).
He gave them the lands of the nations “that they might keep his statutes and observe his laws. Praise the LORD!” (vv. 44-45).
interpretation:
Psalm 105 is a retelling of the exodus with all the failures left out. This is not dishonest. It is a different purpose. Psalm 106 is a confession. Psalm 105 is a thanksgiving. Both are true. The Bible does not hide Israel’s sin, and it does not let sin have the last word.

Notice first who the main actor is. “He sent Moses.” “He brought out Israel.” “He spread a cloud.” “He brought quail.” “He opened the rock.” In the whole passage, God is the subject of almost every verb. Israel is the object. The psalmist is retelling the exodus as a story of what God did. That is the right way to read it. The story is not primarily about Moses’ courage or Israel’s faith. It is about God’s power and faithfulness.

The reason is given in verse 42: “For he remembered his holy promise, and Abraham, his servant.” This verse is the key to the whole book of Exodus. In 2:24, God heard their groaning and remembered his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Here, centuries later, the psalmist says the same: he remembered. The exodus was not a rescue of convenience. It was the fulfillment of a promise made generations before.

Verse 37 is a nice detail. “There was none among his tribes who stumbled.” The whole company of Israel, old, young, sick, and weak, walked out of Egypt without anyone falling behind. God’s redemption is complete. No one is lost.

The ending sets out the purpose of the entire exodus. God gave them the land “that they might keep his statutes and observe his laws.” This brings you back to Sinai. The goal of redemption is a people who obey. This is not to earn the redemption but to live as the redeemed. And the response to all of it is the one word that closes the psalm: “Praise the LORD!”

Placed here, at the end of the unit, the psalm looks forward as well. The God who remembered Abraham and kept his word to Israel will remember his covenant again and send a greater redeemer.
connection: Luke 1:72-73 sings the same note at the birth of Jesus: God “has remembered his holy covenant, the oath that he swore to our father Abraham.” Peter says that Christ’s death was foreknown and planned (1 Peter 1:18-20). Hebrews 2:15 says Christ came “to deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery.” Revelation 15 and 16 echo the plagues and the song of Moses.
application:
Make a list of ways God has been faithful to a promise in your life or in the life of your church. Praise him for each one.

Notice how the psalm ends with obedience. Ask what a response of gratitude would look like in your daily choices.

Say the last word of the psalm out loud: “Praise the LORD!” Do it at least once today, on purpose.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for being faithful to every word he has spoken.
Thank him for the greater exodus in Jesus.
Ask him to help you keep his statutes out of gratitude.
